**Corporate Overview** 

# **Approach to Reporting** 

IndusInd Bank is among India’s leading financial institutions, with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) principles forming an integral part of its operations, risk assessment, and reporting practices. The Bank’s commitment to long-term value creation has been reflected in its proactive sustainability disclosures, dating back to 2011. A significant milestone in this journey was the release of its first Integrated Report (IR) in 2017, which established a strong foundation for subsequent disclosures. Over the years, the Bank’s Integrated Reports have offered a thorough view of its strategy, performance, stakeholder relationships, value creation efforts, and ESG approach. 

# **Reporting Framework** 

This report has been prepared in accordance with the Integrated Reporting (IR) framework prescribed by the International Integrated Reporting Council (IIRC), which has since been merged into the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) Foundation. In addition, the report incorporates disclosures aligned with the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards: Core Option, the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD), and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (UN SDGs). 

# **Reporting Scope and Boundary** 

This report covers the Bank’s financial and non-financial performance across its various business verticals for the period April 1, 2025, to March 31, 2026. 

# **Board of Directors’ Assurance** 

The Bank’s Board of Directors and Senior Management have reviewed this report to ensure it is accurate, complete, and relevant, and in line with the requirements of the <IR> Framework. 

# **Precautionary Principle** 

As a financial institution, the Bank’s ecological influence stems primarily from its operations and loan portfolio. The Bank actively manages and mitigates its carbon footprint while working closely with clients and suppliers to address their environmental and social impact. Additionally, the Bank remains committed to building awareness among its employees on the importance and implications of ESG factors, reinforcing its dedication to sustainable practices.

# **Dear Shareholders,** 

It is a privilege to address you for the first time as the Chairman of IndusInd Bank. 

FY2025–26 was a year marked by both resilience and renewal. The global economy navigated a complex landscape shaped by geopolitical tensions, policy uncertainty, and evolving macroeconomic conditions. Despite these headwinds, India continued to distinguish itself as one of the world’s fastestgrowing major economies, supported by strong fundamentals, macroeconomic stability, and resilient domestic demand. 

Global economic activity displayed resilience despite elevated policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, and high import tariffs. While the impact of the US tariff measures proved less severe than initially anticipated, fiscal support in advanced economies, together with strong technology-led investments and trade, supported growth. The military conflict in West Asia once again tested the resilience of the global economy, driving oil prices higher and reinforcing geopolitical risk as a key drag on global growth. 

The IMF projects global growth of 3.1% in 2026, lower than earlier estimates, while inflation is expected to remain elevated. Although the global economy has demonstrated resilience, disparities across economies persist, particularly for net energy importers. The gradual normalisation of energy supplies from the Middle East following the extension of the ceasefire between the US and Iran should help moderate these pressures, although the outlook continues to depend on the duration and intensity of energy price and supply disruptions. 

Amid these global uncertainties, the Indian economy demonstrated remarkable resilience. Supported by fiscal measures, monetary policy easing, and adequate foreign exchange reserves, it remained on a strong growth trajectory. Macroeconomic and financial stability, together with benign inflation, continued to support private consumption and fixed investment, while GST rationalisation, lower policy rates, and the Reserve Bank of India’s liquidity measures further strengthened domestic demand and credit growth. 

**Equally significant was the renewed emphasis on governance and oversight. The learnings from past developments have been thoughtfully internalised, resulting in stronger internal controls, sharper risk management practices, and enhanced accountability. Working closely with the Management, the Board has sought to embed a culture anchored in integrity, transparency, and discipline, recognising governance not merely as a framework for oversight but as the foundation of sound decision-making and long-term institutional strength.** 

Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 07 

**Reflecting these strong fundamentals, real GDP growth accelerated to 7.7% in FY2025–26 from 7.1% in the previous year. Recognising India’s robust long-term growth prospects and improving public finances, S&P upgraded India’s sovereign rating to BBB in August, 2025, marking the country’s first sovereign rating upgrade in 18 years.** 

The banking sector also maintained strong momentum. Bank credit grew 16% year-on-year as of March 31, 2026, supported by benign CPI inflation, lower policy rates, and ample liquidity. The Union Budget’s significant policy shift to a Debt-to-GDP framework as the fiscal anchor represents an important step towards strengthening the countercyclical role of fiscal policy, balancing support for growth with fiscal consolidation, while maintaining its continued emphasis on capital expenditure. While downside risks to growth and upside risks to inflation remain, India’s strong domestic fundamentals and continued policy support position the economy well to navigate an uncertain global environment. 

For IndusInd Bank, FY2025–26 marked an important inflection point in its journey and was a period of institutional strengthening, reflection, transition, purposeful recalibration, renewal, and purposeful action. Against a backdrop of macroeconomic resilience, evolving geopolitical developments, and sectoral challenges, particularly within parts of unsecured lending, the Board and Management remained steadfast in their commitment to strengthening governance, enhancing risk and control frameworks, deepening leadership capabilities, improving balance sheet resilience, and reinforcing the Bank’s institutional foundations. Guided by prudence, discipline, and a long-term perspective, these efforts have positioned the Bank to move forward with renewed confidence and a clear focus on creating sustainable long-term value for all stakeholders. 



A key development during the year was the leadership transition, with the appointment of the Managing Director & CEO, and the strengthening of senior management team across key business and control functions. This transition was managed with continuity and stability while bringing renewed perspective, deeper domain expertise, and sharper execution capability. With the leadership team now largely in place, your Bank is well positioned to move from a phase of transition to one of focused execution and sustained progress. 

Equally significant was the renewed emphasis on governance and oversight. The learnings from past developments have been thoughtfully internalised, resulting in stronger internal controls, sharper risk management practices, and enhanced accountability. Working closely with the Management, the Board has sought to embed a culture anchored in integrity, transparency, and discipline, recognising governance not merely as a framework for oversight but as the foundation of sound decision-making and long-term institutional strength. 

From a business perspective, FY2025–26 was characterised by a deliberate strengthening of the balance sheet to reinforce resilience and create a robust platform for sustainable growth. Your Bank adopted a calibrated approach to growth, rebalancing the portfolio towards granular and secured segments while enhancing the quality and stability of its funding base. Supported by a healthy Capital Adequacy Ratio of 17.48% and a Liquidity Coverage Ratio of 118%, the Bank remains well capitalised and financially resilient. The financial performance for the year reflects your Bank’s strategic choice of prioritising long-term strength over near-term expansion. While profitability reflected elevated credit costs during the year, early signs of stabilisation in the microfinance portfolio and improving fundamentals position your Bank well for a gradual recovery and sustainable growth in FY2026–27.

Customer-centricity and execution excellence will remain central to the Bank’s strategy, enabling it to deliver consistent service, improve productivity, and achieve stronger business outcomes. Technology and data and analytics will continue to play an increasingly important role in supporting the Bank’s strategic priorities.

During the year, the Bank continued to advance its ‘One IndusInd’ strategy, strengthening customer centricity, driving greater collaboration across businesses, and building a more integrated franchise. Digital adoption gained further momentum, underscoring the increasing acceptance of the Bank’s digital channels and technology-led solutions. 

We also continued to invest in technology, data, and AI-driven capabilities to enhance customer experience, strengthen risk management, and improve organisational effectiveness. Combined with efforts to improve portfolio quality and optimise the business mix, these initiatives are helping build a more resilient, diversified, and future-ready institution. 

This commitment is reflected in the way your Bank serves communities across the country. Marking a significant milestone, the Bank’s CSR initiatives have positively impacted nearly 25 Lakh lives during FY2025–26, primarily through initiatives focused on economic empowerment.

I conclude by extending my sincere gratitude to all our stakeholders - customers, investors, employees, regulators, media, and partner institutions, for their unwavering support, trust, and belief.

# **MESSAGE FROM THE MANAGING DIRECTOR &** **<u>CEO</u>** 

### **Dear Shareholders,** 

I am writing to you for the first time through the Annual Report as Managing Director & CEO of IndusInd Bank at a significant moment in the Bank’s journey. 

FY2026 tested the Bank’s resilience, clarified its priorities, and created an opportunity to strengthen the institution for the long term. For any enduring financial institution, moments of change are important not merely because they demand a response, but because they reveal the quality of its foundations. 

When I assumed this responsibility in August 2025, I was deeply conscious of the trust placed in me. My interactions with customers, employees, regulators, shareholders, and partners have reinforced a simple conviction. Institutions endure when they combine ambition with discipline. Markets, technologies, and business cycles will continue to evolve. But the constants of banking remain trust, relationships, values, and the quality of execution. 

This conviction shaped our choices. We have strengthened governance and oversight, refreshed leadership across the organisation, reinforced risk and compliance practices, and placed greater emphasis on asset quality, capital, liquidity, and customer trust. Together, these measures provide a stronger platform for sustainable performance and long-term value creation. 

## **A New Leadership Team for a New Era of Growth** 

Today, IndusInd Bank is being led by a renewed leadership team across its business and control functions. The Board has also been strengthened to provide enhanced oversight and stewardship. 

We have appointed seasoned leaders with deep domain expertise and diverse industry experiences. Each brings a fresh perspective and simplifies decision-making by ensuring that business and control functions are aligned. The Bank is primed to accelerate execution of strategic priorities and build a resilient, future-ready institution supported by the Board and the management team. 

Our mandate is clear: protect the strengths that have made IndusInd Bank distinctive, bring greater rigour in execution capabilities, and build a culture of accountability, collaboration, and execution excellence. 

## **Operating with Clarity in a Changing Environment** 

The year unfolded amid global uncertainty. Geopolitical shifts, changing trade patterns, policy changes, and rapid technological advances driven by artificial intelligence created a complex environment for economies and markets to navigate. 

Despite these headwinds, India stood out as a resilient long-term growth story, with real GDP growth of 7.7% supported by strong domestic demand and private consumption. This resilience was also reflected in the Banking sector, with credit growth of 16%. While the outlook continues to be influenced by geopolitical developments and the impact of El Niño, the Indian economy remains well-positioned. The Government and the Reserve Bank of India’s efforts to support growth while maintaining price stability continue to create lending opportunities for the Banking sector. Strong domestic demand, coupled with the Government’s sustained infrastructure push, with budgeted capital expenditure of over ₹12 Lakh crore, further reinforces this outlook.

India’s banking system continues to operate from a position of strength, supported by sound capitalisation, adequate liquidity, improving asset quality, and sustained regulatory oversight. In this environment, the Reserve Bank of India’s continued focus on governance, risk management, customer protection, and digital resilience has reinforced an important principle for the sector: growth must be responsible, transparent, and well-governed. 

For IndusInd Bank, this environment sharpened our choices. It reaffirmed that sustainable growth cannot be built by pursuing every opportunity. It must be built through sound governance, prudent risk management, consistent execution, and deep customer trust. 

# **FY2026: Choosing Strength Over Speed** 

FY2026 was a year of transition, recalibration, and renewal for IndusInd Bank. Throughout the year, we consciously prioritised balance sheet strength, asset quality, and long-term sustainability over near-term growth. 

We undertook a comprehensive review of our business and operating model. This included tightening underwriting standards, improving the quality and resilience of our portfolio mix, reinforcing risk management practices, and embedding greater operating rigour across the organisation. These choices moderated growth and impacted profitability in the near term, but they have enhanced the quality and durability of the franchise. 

The Bank’s strategy is guided by a three-year roadmap. The first year is centred on strengthening the Bank’s foundations, restoring the franchise to industry-aligned growth and achieving an exit Return on Assets (RoA) of 1% in FY2027. The second year will focus on scaling the business and accelerating growth momentum, while the third year is intended to deliver outperformance by building leadership positions across selected business segments. 

The Bank enhanced its deposit franchise with a focus on mobilising retail deposits. We redesigned customer-facing processes, improved the onboarding journey, and reduced account-activation turnaround time. At the same time, we accelerated channel integration to leverage synergies. These steps helped us close FY2026 with total deposits of ₹3,99,931 crore. The share of retail deposits improved to 47.9% from 46.6% in the previous financial year, supported by robust, new-to-bank CASA acquisitions and healthy growth across our NRI and Affluent Banking franchise. 

Our loan book stood at ₹3.15 Lakh crore year-on-year as the Bank pursued balance sheet optimisation by shedding inefficient assets, growing core retail assets, and adopting a risk-adjusted approach to allocation of capital for growth. The focus was on reinforcing the traditionally strong areas like vehicle financing, scaling consumer banking assets, prioritising risk-adjusted returns for wholesale banking, and targeting white spaces within the Bank such as MSMEs and rural banking. With asset quality stabilising, FY2027 will be a year of calibrated growth rather than a contraction in micro loans. 

Overall, asset quality continued to improve during the year, with GNPA and net NPA at 3.43% and 1.00%, respectively. 

The Bank reported a consolidated pre-provision operating profit of ₹9,180 crore and a Profit After Tax of ₹889 crore for FY2025–26. The underlying trends are encouraging, with annualised RoA improving to 0.45% in Q4 FY26, compared to 0.17% for FY26 as a whole. Our capital and liquidity position remained robust throughout the year with a healthy Capital Adequacy Ratio (CRAR) of 17.48%, a Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR) of 71%, and a Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) of 118%, comfortably above regulatory requirements. 

The trends in asset quality, retail deposits, and operating leverage, a more resilient funding profile, and a robust capital position give us confidence in progressively improving returns over the medium term, positioning the Bank on a stronger footing for sustainable long-term growth. 

# **Strengthening the Franchise** 



Alongside these improvements, we continued to deepen customer-centricity, accelerate digital innovation, and foster greater collaboration across businesses. 

A key pillar of this transformation is the ‘One IndusInd’ experience – serving customers as an integrated Bank that delivers a unified and consistent experience across every touchpoint. We are transitioning from product-led banking to relationship-led 

12 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 

**Corporate Overview** 

engagement by integrating products, channels, and businesses, while progressively transforming specialised branches into full-service banking outlets in suitable locations. This enables us to leverage our existing distribution network more effectively, unlock greater synergies across our asset, and liability franchises, and build deeper, more enduring customer relationships. 

Vehicle Finance, one of the Bank’s key pillars, maintained growth momentum with the loan book reaching ₹99,876 crore. Asset quality in this segment improved, supported by a sustained focus on collections and recoveries. We also strengthened the franchise by integrating nearly 300 vehicle branches with our branch banking network, enhancing customer reach, improving productivity, and creating a more seamless banking experience. Our strategic objective in this segment is to strengthen our leadership position across vehicle categories and drive marketshare gains in the coming years. 

The Rural Banking business demonstrated encouraging signs of recovery. The Microfinance portfolio witnessed improvement in asset quality, validating our strengthened underwriting models and providing the confidence to progressively scale microfinance disbursements while maintaining prudent risk discipline. We also continued to diversify our rural franchise, with our merchant loan book growing 11% year-on-year to over 570K merchant borrowers, and our affordable housing portfolio growing 24% year-on-year, alongside expansion in Kisan Credit and other rural lending segments, positioning the business for more stable and sustainable growth. 

Consumer Banking continued its strategic shift towards secured retail lending, delivering strong momentum across key segments. The home loan portfolio grew 45% year-on-year to ₹6,510 crore, while the gold loan franchise crossed the ₹1,000 crore milestone, after monthly disbursements tripled over the past six months. Overall consumer banking assets grew 8% yearon-year, supported by disciplined underwriting and improving asset quality. 

The SME franchise continued to strengthen during the year, with the loan book reaching ₹44,347 crore. As one of India’s largest and structurally attractive growth opportunities, the segment remains central to our long-term strategy. We realigned our SME coverage model and strengthened our operating processes, risk frameworks and execution capabilities to deliver a more integrated ‘One Bank, One Customer’ experience, positioning the business to capture long-term growth while maintaining portfolio resilience. 

Digital continued to support growth and service. Our direct digital business model scaled meaningfully, with digitally acquired assets book growing 19% year-on-year.  We successfully migrated customers to our unified mobile banking platform, which now serves a registered user base of 4.8 million with a robust Monthly Active User (MAU) rate of 58%, reflecting strong customer engagement. We continue to invest in AI-native capabilities to deliver differentiated digital banking experiences, anchored in hyper-personalisation, innovation, trust, and security, while delivering a seamless experience across our web and mobile platforms and simplifying customer journeys. Our digital proposition for MSMEs also gained strong traction, with growing payment transaction volumes reflecting its increasing adoption as a primary operating account. We also expanded our international banking presence through GIFT City, reinforcing our long-term ambition of building a diversified, technology-led and future-ready institution. 

# **Keeping Customers at the Centre** 

Every decision we make is ultimately guided by one question: does it improve the value, protection, or experience we provide to our customers? 

Trust is earned through every interaction. During the year, we reinforced fair conduct standards, enhanced transparency, strengthened fraud monitoring capabilities, and accelerated the resolution of customer grievances. While these are operational improvements, they reflect our commitment to delivering banking that is secure, transparent, and dependable. 

**We reimagined key customer journeys to make banking simpler, faster, and more intuitive. Assisted digital accountopening turnaround times were reduced by 80% for Savings Accounts and 63% for Current Accounts.** 

The integration of our branch banking and vehicle finance networks enhanced customer convenience, improved productivity, and enabled stronger engagement across our retail franchise. These efforts also contributed to a 35% growth in deposits sourced from vehicle finance customers during the year. 

Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 13 

Alongside these initiatives, we continued to leverage data-led insights and emerging technologies to deliver more relevant and personalised experiences. As customer expectations continue to evolve, our responsibility is not only to keep pace with change, but also to anticipate it and continuously raise the standards we set for ourselves. 

# **Building a Future-Ready Bank in the Age of AI** 

Artificial intelligence is reshaping how decisions are made, how risk is assessed, how operations are run, and how customers experience financial services. We see AI as a means to strengthen judgement, improve service, and deliver better and consistent outcomes, not as technology for its own sake. 

During the year, we established a dedicated Business Intelligence Unit and AI Centre of Excellence, to further strengthen our data capabilities and provide leadership oversight to accelerate the responsible adoption of AI. 

Ten high-impact Gen-AI initiatives were rolled out across sales productivity, conversational banking and service, credit underwriting, and collections, enhancing customer experience, risk management and enterprise productivity. 

The Bank has a suite of 50+ machine learning models which supports the assessment of nearly 5,00,000 loan applications each month, strengthening underwriting consistency and portfolio quality while reducing credit decision turnaround. The Bank’s ML-based recommendation engine enables Relationship Managers to identify and deliver more relevant cross-sell and upsell opportunities to millions of customers, while enterprise AI tools are enhancing employee productivity. 

We are also scaling AI across collections, fraud monitoring, decision support, and operational processes, while investing in data architecture and people capability. For financial crime prevention, machine learning models monitor transactions 

across millions of customers every hour, generating alerts for human investigators, thus strengthening our fraud detection capabilities, and leading to a significant improvement in the detection of credit card fraud. 

Besides a centralised Business Intelligence Unit and AI Centre of Excellence, the Bank has also invested in a modern data and AI platform. The platform holds a petabyte scale data lake house, with ability to develop and deploy ML models, AI agents, AI applications, and conversational dashboards. With 500+ users, this platform provides the Bank with technology platform to deliver in the age of AI. 

As these capabilities expand, responsible use is non-negotiable. Human oversight, data privacy, model governance, security, and regulatory compliance will remain integral to how we design and deploy AI. Technology must strengthen, not weaken, the relationships and trust at the heart of banking. 

# **Culture, Execution, and P.A.C.E.** 

Strategy succeeds when culture, systems, and people move in the same direction. That is why our organisational transformation is focused not only on structure, but on behaviour: ownership, accountability, agility, collaboration, integrity, customer focus, and disciplined execution. 

To guide the next phase of our journey, we have articulated a clear strategic roadmap: P.A.C.E. 

## **Protect the Endowments** 

Build on our core strengths in vehicle finance, rural banking, and corporate banking by enhancing risk management, deepening customer relationships, and adapting to changing market dynamics. 

## **Accelerate Key Priorities** 

Scale granular deposits and expand retail and SME businesses, with emphasis on improving the mix, quality, and sustainability of growth. 

## **Customer Centricity** 

Deliver a more seamless and consistent customer experience by using digital and AI capabilities and data-led insights to better serve evolving customer needs. 



## **Execution Excellence** 

Drive stronger accountability, improve operational efficiency, and maintain disciplined cost management to ensure consistent delivery of our strategic priorities. 

14 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 

**Corporate Overview** 

Our FY2027–FY2029 roadmap follows a phased approach: stability in the first year, calibrated scale-up in the second, and a clear aspiration to deliver industry out-performance in the third. Together, these priorities will help us build a stronger institution, supported by a diversified business model, prudent risk management, and consistent execution. 

# **Responsible Banking, Sustainable Growth** 

Sustainability remains integral to how we create long-term value. Our sustainable finance portfolio, which accounted for 47.43% of total advances during the year FY2025-26, reflects our continued commitment to financing responsible and inclusive growth. We also strengthened partnerships with development finance institutions, funds, and foundations to expand access to capital for underserved communities and advance inclusive development. Our progress in embedding sustainability across the organisation was reflected in strong ESG ratings, reaffirming the strength of our responsible banking framework. 

FY2026 also marked an important milestone in our CSR journey. Through focused interventions across livelihoods, education, sustainable environment, and economic empowerment, we positively impacted nearly 25 Lakh lives during the year. Our initiatives continued to improve access to water in rural communities, particularly benefiting women who are often the primary water managers within households. Our Holistic Rural Development Programme delivered measurable outcomes, including an approximately 30% increase in household income across participating communities. 

Our Education and Employability initiatives supported more than 7,600 entrepreneurs, including over 6,800 women entrepreneurs, and created opportunities for persons with disabilities and armed forces veterans. Under Bharat Sanjeevani, women-led community cadres such as Pashu Sakhis played a vital role in delivering last-mile services, supporting over 3 Lakh farmers directly and strengthening inclusive livelihood ecosystems. We also continued to champion inclusion through sport by 

supporting para-athletes and visually impaired athletes, with the Indian Women’s Blind Cricket Team scripting history by winning the inaugural T20 Blind Cricket World Cup. Together, these initiatives reflect our belief that sustainable development is most meaningful when individuals and communities are empowered not merely as beneficiaries, but as active participants in creating lasting social and economic progress. 

Our commitment to innovation, customer-centricity, and responsible banking continued to attract external recognition during the year. The Bank was recognised by the Department of Financial Services, Ministry of Finance, for Outstanding Performance in Digital Payments and was also named Best Technology Bank at the Indian Banks’ Association’s 21<sup>st</sup> Annual Banking Technology Awards, reaffirming the progress we are making in strengthening our digital capabilities while delivering meaningful outcomes for customers and society. 

# **Closing Remarks** 

I would like to express my sincere gratitude to our customers, shareholders, regulators, Board members, and employees for their trust, partnership, and support throughout this defining year. 

We begin this next chapter with stronger foundations, clearer priorities, a leadership team aligned on execution, and a sound capital and liquidity position. The work ahead will require rigor and focus. It also presents significant opportunity. 

IndusInd Bank has always been built by people who believed in moving forward with conviction. As we look to the future, we do so with the same spirit and a renewed commitment to building an institution that is stronger, more trusted, and future-ready. 

Warm regards, 

**Rajiv Anand, Managing Director & CEO**

### **OUR HISTORY** 

Established in 1994, IndusInd Bank was founded with a vision to build a world-class private sector bank that would combine financial strength with a deep commitment to serving India’s growing aspirations. The Bank is guided by enduring values of integrity, trust, and nation building. Our listing on the stock exchanges marked an important milestone in our journey, reinforcing the confidence of investors and providing a strong platform for sustainable growth. Over the years, we have steadily expanded our footprint, with the milestone of crossing our first 1,000 branches in FY2016, signalling the scale of our nationwide presence. Today, we are India’s fifthlargest private sector bank, serving more than 42 million customers through a network of over 3,000 branches across the country.

**01 02 A Distribution Moat Built on Last-Mile Reach Memory**

**03** 

**A Proprietary Rural Credit Infrastructure** 

#### **Physical presence at a scale and depth that cannot be assembled quickly** 

Most private sector banks in India have concentrated their distribution in metropolitan and urban geographies, where acquisition costs are lower and average ticket sizes are larger. IndusInd Bank has made a structurally different choice. Through our own branch network and the field infrastructure of Bharat Financial Inclusion Limited (BFIL), we maintain active credit and banking relationships across approximately 1.62 Lakh villages in 23 states, a rural footprint that few institutions of comparable size have attempted to build. 

#### **Domain expertise and market relationships accumulated over multiple credit cycles** 

What distinguishes us is the institutional depth behind it. Over 30+ years, we have developed proprietary underwriting models calibrated to the income patterns, asset utilisation cycles, and credit behaviour of commercial vehicle operators, a customer segment characterised by irregular cash flows, asset-backed repayment capacity, and strong collateral but limited formal documentation. 

#### **A self-contained origination, servicing, and collection system for underserved segments** 

Our rural banking business is not a distribution extension of our mainstream retail franchise. It operates through a structurally distinct platform, BFIL, with its own field workforce, centrebased credit methodology, and community relationship architecture. This platform serves borrowing merchants, micro-entrepreneurs, agricultural households, and self-help group members across geographies where conventional branch banking is economically unviable.

**A Credit Cycle Reset With Conservative Provisioning** 

## **A funding base that is becoming more resilient, not merely larger** 

The quality of a bank’s liability franchise is determined solely by the stability of our composition and the cost at which funding is secured. IndusInd Bank has made deliberate progress on both dimensions. This shift toward granular retail funding reduces reliance on institutional and wholesale deposits, which are more rate-sensitive and more susceptible to withdrawals during periods of market stress. 

We are pursuing retail liability deepening through four reinforcing channels: a ‘One Bank’ integrated service model, premium and differentiated product offerings for affluent and NRI segments, digital acquisition through INDIE, and the rural Bharat Money Store network. These channels address different customer segments simultaneously, structurally improving deposit granularity without dependence on any single acquisition lever. 

## **Digital infrastructure that generates engagement, origination, and data advantages simultaneously** 

INDIE and INDIE for Business constitute an integrated digital banking ecosystem that serves as an acquisition channel, a servicing platform, a product distribution engine, and a source of behavioural data, simultaneously. This multi-function architecture creates compounding value that a single-purpose digital channel cannot replicate. 

As of March 31, 2026, INDIE had 4.8 million registrations, with 2.8 million monthly active users and a 58% monthly active user rate among registered customers. 

## **A balance sheet that has absorbed stress, not deferred it** 

The Bank entered FY26 carrying elevated credit stress concentrated in the microfinance and unsecured retail segments, ref lec ting industr y-wide deterioration in those portfolios. The response—a deliberate combination of tightened underwriting, aggressive writeoffs, and sustained provisioning— has resulted in a measurable improvement in asset quality metrics by the end of the financial year, with the provisioning buffer maintained at a conservative level.

## **Operating Context** 

# **POISED FOR GROWTH IN A RECALIBRATING LANDSCAPE** 

**In FY2026, IndusInd Bank operated in an environment shaped by strong domestic economic momentum, a decisive shift in monetary policy, the continued acceleration of digital payments, tightening ESG regulatory frameworks, and an evolving microfinance landscape moving towards recovery.** 

Against this backdrop, we absorbed legacy headwinds, stabilised our fundamentals, and positioned ourselves for the next phase of sustainable growth. 

38 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26

39 

# **INDIA’S ECONOMIC MOMENTUM CREATED RENEWED OPPORTUNITY** 

India’s real GDP is estimated to have grown 7.4% in FY2026. This momentum was broad-based, with manufacturing growing 9.1%, construction rising 7.2%, and financial, real estate, and professional services registering 10.2% growth in Q2 FY2026. 

Along with consumption, investment has continued to anchor growth in FY2026, with the share of Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF) estimated at 30%. 

Strong domestic demand and household consumption supported by income tax cuts and increased government infrastructure spending were the primary engines of growth. 

# **A SUPPORTIVE MONETARY CYCLE IMPROVED TRANSMISSION AND MARGINS** 

The RBI delivered a cumulative 125 basis points of rate cuts through FY2026, bringing the repo rate down to 5.25% by December 2025, in a decisive shift from its earlier tightening stance. This easing cycle was supported by benign inflation, which fell to 1.33% in December 2025, comfortably below the RBI’s 2-6% tolerance band. At the same time, the RBI maintained heightened scrutiny on asset quality, unsecured credit growth, and governance practices across the Banking sector, raising the bar for disclosures and risk management. 

Source: **BankBazaar** 

Source: **PIB** 

## **The Bank’s Response** 

Against this supportive macroeconomic backdrop, we sharpened our strategic focus on quality growth over volume. The Bank maintained a well-diversified loan book of ₹3,15,871 crore, with a deliberate shift towards retail and SME segments, which together comprised 66% of the total portfolio. Vehicle Finance, a domain of over 35 years of vintage and market leadership, grew 4% year-on-year. Capital Adequacy was reinforced to 17.48%, positioning the Bank with the headroom to participate in India’s growth trajectory in a measured and disciplined manner. 

## **The Bank’s Response** 

The Bank focused on improving both funding mix and cost profile. The share of average retail deposits as per LCR improved to 47.9% in Q4 FY2026 vs 46.6% in Q4 FY2025. The cost of fund improved 5.14% in Q4FY2026 vs 5.6% in Q4 FY2025.

# **DIGITAL PAYMENTS MOVED TO MAINSTREAM INFRASTRUCTURE** 

UPI processed over 24,162 crore transactions in FY2026, representing an almost 12,000-fold surge in volume since its launch in FY2017. UPI now commands nearly 85% of India’s total digital payment volume, with nearly 66 crore transactions recorded daily, valued at approximately ₹0.86 Lakh crore. Digital payment transactions accounted for 99.7% of total transaction volume in India’s payments system in 2024, with the trend continuing into the first half of 2025, according to the RBI’s Payment System Report. Digital banking moved firmly from adoption to habit across urban and rural segments alike. 

Source: **Press Information Bureau** 

# **ESG REGULATION MOVED FROM VOLUNTARY TO STRUCTURAL** 

In June 2025, SEBI introduced a formal framework for ESG-labelled debt securities covering social bonds, sustainability bonds, and sustainability-linked bonds, making third-party reviews and post-issuance reporting mandatory. The RBI’s Climate Disclosure Framework, set for implementation in FY2026, required banks to prepare for mandatory climate-related financial disclosures. For the 2025-26 reporting cycle, value chain accountability and green finance integrity became central themes, with SEBI mandating the top 250 listed entities to disclose ESG performance across their value chains. ESG integration shifted from signalling intent to demonstrating performance. 

Source: **Down To Earth**

# **WAY FORWARD: P.A.C.E. STRATEGY TO DRIVE SUSTAINABLE GROWTH** 

During the year, the Bank articulated its three-year strategic roadmap – **P.A.C.E.** , which provides a clear framework to build an all-weather banking franchise and deliver sustainable and profitable growth: 

**1** 

## **Protect the Endowments** 

Strengthen and preserve our core franchises including Vehicle Finance, Rural Banking, Corporate Relationships, Payments, and Transaction Banking. These businesses provide differentiated market positions, deep customer relationships, and strong ecosystem linkages that will continue to serve as important engines of growth. 

**2** 

## **Accelerate Key Priorities** 

Build a more granular and diversified balance sheet by strengthening retail deposits and CASA, deepening relationships across retail, affluent, NRI, entrepreneur, and SME segments, and scaling high-quality secured lending businesses. We will also focus on expanding SME and mid-market banking, increasing customer primacy and improving the quality and sustainability of growth across the franchise. 

**3** 

## **Customer Centricity** 

Deliver a unified **“One IndusInd”** experience through integrated propositions, seamless customer journeys, and superior service delivery across channels. By combining relationship-led engagement with data-driven insights, we aim to deepen customer relationships and become the preferred banking partner across personal and business banking needs. 

## **4** 

## **Execution Excellence** 

Drive a culture of strong execution discipline, sharper accountability, and continuous productivity improvement. We will continue to invest in digital transformation, data and AI-enabled capabilities, automation, and straight-through processing to improve customer experience, enhance operational efficiency, and create a scalable platform for growth. At the same time, strong governance, compliance, and risk management will remain central to our operating philosophy, ensuring that growth is pursued responsibly and sustainably. 

# **LOOKING AHEAD** 

With a strengthened leadership team, a more resilient balance sheet, improving portfolio trends, and a clearly defined strategic roadmap, the Bank is well positioned to rebuild momentum and accelerate growth. Our focus remains on building an all-weather banking franchise through granular liabilities, high-quality asset growth, digital and AI-led transformation, strong governance, and disciplined execution, creating sustainable long-term value for customers, shareholders, and all stakeholders.

## **Materiality** 

# **THE ART OF MATERIAL FOCUS** 

**IndusInd Bank applies materiality as a structured mechanism to identify and prioritise the issues that are most consequential to our stakeholders and our business.** 

The operating environment continues to be shaped by macroeconomic change, accelerating digital adoption, regulatory development, and growing expectations around ESG performance. The materiality assessment is designed to keep us aligned with these shifts while maintaining strategic focus and institutional discipline. 

46 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 

**Corporate Overview** 

# **THE MATERIALITY ASSESSMENT PROCESS** 

Our materiality process integrates stakeholder perspectives, sector-level developments, and internal strategic priorities to identify issues of significance. The output is reviewed periodically to ensure continued relevance and is used to inform both reporting boundaries and management decisions. This approach ensures that materiality functions as a governance tool, not merely a disclosure requirement. 



<!-- Start of picture text -->
Define purpose<br>and scope<br><!-- End of picture text -->



Assess the impact of each topic on our business and on stakeholders 



<!-- Start of picture text -->
Identify potential  Map out key<br>material topics stakeholder groups<br>Engage with stakeholders  Establish and validate the<br>to prioritise issues materiality matrix<br><!-- End of picture text -->

This process draws from global best practices, including the GRI Standards, <IR> Framework, and SEBI-BRSR guidelines. 

# **MATERIALITY MATRIX** 

IndusInd Bank reviewed and validated 19 material topics for FY2026. Each topic was assessed against two criteria: its impact on the Bank’s business, and its significance to stakeholders. The output is represented through a materiality matrix that provides a structured basis for prioritisation across reporting and management decisions.

# **A NETWORK RECALIBRATED FOR QUALITY OF REACH** 

IndusInd Bank closed FY2026 with 9,535 touch points across India, comprising 3,136 branches and banking outlets, 3,427 BFIL branches, 102 Vehicle Finance marketing outlets, and 2,870 ATMs. The reduction from prior period levels reflects governance-led rationalisation rather than a retreat from market presence. 

The branch network’s geographic composition reflects a balanced national footprint: South 27%, North 22%, East 20%, West 18%, and Central 13%. By settlement type—Metro 28%, Urban 25%, Semi-Urban 23%, Rural 24%—we continue to serve customers across the full spectrum of Indian geographies. 

BFIL’s branch consolidation was the most significant component of this rationalisation, a deliberate response to sector-wide microfinance stress that prioritised relationship quality over network expansion. Despite the reduction in outlet count, BFIL’s reach remained substantial, approximately 1.62 Lakh across 23 states, 85,000+ active Bharat Money Stores, and 5.7 Lakh borrowing merchants. By year-end, disbursement momentum had recovered measurably, and net collection efficiency for current customers returned to near-peak levels, confirming that a smaller network was performing with greater rigour. Vehicle Finance marketing outlets were similarly rationalised, consistent with the Bank’s focus on quality origination within a franchise that has held leadership across vehicle categories for over 35 years. 

# **GOVERNANCE CLOSURE AS STRUCTURAL ACHIEVEMENT** 

The Board-mandated Project Management Group concluded its work during the year, completing the implementation of enhanced controls across reconciliation, manual accounting entries, and internal reporting frameworks. The Joint Statutory Auditors issued an unmodified audit opinion on the FY2026 financial results, a formal attestation of the integrity of the Bank’s financial reporting infrastructure. Accountability processes were concluded for the majority of officials involved in prior-year discrepancies.

INDIE recorded 4.8 million+ cumulative registrations and 2.8 million+ monthly active users as of March 2026, with 6.6 million+ transactions processed monthly. ## **INDIE: FROM PLATFORM TO ECOSYSTEM** 

What began as a flagship app has become the definitive expression of what IndusInd Bank stands for in retail banking. By March 2026, INDIE had crossed **4.8 million registrations and 2.5 million savings account customers,** with **2.8 million monthly active users,** nearly double the engagement base reported a year ago. The app’s MAU rate stood at 58% of the registered base, a strong indicator of stickiness and utility. 

The platform delivered across all three vectors of modern banking: acquisition, engagement, and transactions. In Q4 FY2026 alone, INDIE led over **6.6 million transactions,** processed **1.4 million+ UPI transactions,** handled **490K+ bill payment transactions,** and served **150K+ recurring-transaction active users.** Over I2,767 crore in fixed deposits and recurring deposits were opened through the platform during the quarter. 

INDIE now hosts 100+ banking features across web and mobile, spanning savings accounts, payments, fixed and recurring deposits, line of credit, credit cards, mutual fund investments, and digital servicing. Its differentiated features continue to set it apart: dynamic PINs, virtual disposable cards, super OTPs for low-connectivity zones, smart recurring payment setups, and a unified relationship view for domestic and NRI customers across loans, cards, deposits, and wealth. 

With legacy mobile banking fully phased out during the year, the migration to INDIE is now complete, marking a clean architectural break and a new chapter in how the Bank serves its retail customers.

## **INDIE FOR BUSINESS: SCALING THE BUSINESS BANKING SUPERAPP** 

INDIE for Business came into its own in FY2026. The platform crossed **600K+ registrations** and achieved a **67% MAU rate** among registered customers, validating both its adoption and the depth of engagement it generates. 

Across its entity-agnostic architecture, supporting individual current accounts, sole proprietorships, partnerships, LLPs, private and public limited companies, and one person companies, the app has become a genuine operating platform for India’s MSME community. 

Core capabilities include instant self-registration without branch visits, consolidated loan and repayment views, bulk vendor, and salary payments, real-time cashflow dashboards, and integrated business loan servicing. Our strategy of deploying tailor-made digital offerings alongside strong risk assessment frameworks continues to drive a granular, well-diversified SME portfolio. 

## **A UNIFIED DIGITAL ACQUISITION AND ORIGINATION STACK** 

FY2026 saw the full operationalisation of end-to-end digital journeys across every major retail product. The scale achieved in Q4 alone tells the story: 

# **29K+ savings accounts** opened via fully digital, zero-visit journeys 

# **189K+ term deposits** opened through DIY digital flows 

These numbers reflect the maturation of our video KYC infrastructure, AI-driven credit scoring engines, and integrated martech automation, capabilities built in prior years now operating at sustained scale. 

Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 63 

# **TECHNOLOGY AND INFRASTRUCTURE: CONSOLIDATING THE GAINS** 

The modernisation agenda initiated in FY2025 continued through FY2026, with the focus shifting from transformation to reliability, performance, and governance. 

Our core banking system (Finacle), UPI infrastructure, and treasury systems, all upgraded in the prior year, demonstrated the resilience of the new stack. The UPI microservices architecture, built on public cloud, continued to deliver sub400 ms transaction processing, 99.999% uptime, and real-time reconciliation within 10 minutes of NPCI cycles. Disaster recovery RTO remained under 7 minutes. 

We also made meaningful investments in upgrading our CRM infrastructure, keeping pace with evolving customer preferences across segments, a key enabler of the retailisation strategy being pursued on both the liabilities and assets sides. 

The IBA’s recognition of IndusInd as the **Best Technology Bank** for FY2025, and Special Mentions in AI & ML Adoption and IT Risk Management, validated the multi-year investment in platform modernisation. 

# **INTELLIGENCE AT SCALE: DATA, AI, AND ANALYTICS** 

The Enterprise Data Platform, established in FY2025, built on a medallion architecture with near-real-time ingestion, a 1.5 petabyte data lakehouse, and 100+ source system feeds, continued to power an expanding range of use cases in FY2026. 

Fraud modelling, AI-powered transactional fraud detection across cards, payments, and branches, hyper-personalised marketing and regulatory reporting all draw from this shared intelligence infrastructure. The dedicated BFIL microfinance data platform, offering 360° visibility on the rural loan book, contributed to sharper collection strategies and more predictive credit behaviour modelling, supporting the meaningful improvement in microfinance slippages seen through the year. 

Improved risk and analytical models were highlighted as a key driver in the Consumer Banking franchise, enabling better sourcing decisions and portfolio quality management across home loans, personal loans, and other retail assets. 

# **SECURITY BY DESIGN** 

As digital adoption deepened, IndusInd Bank’s security posture strengthened in parallel. Micro-segmentation for high-risk applications, IAM, SIEM, EDR and MDR frameworks, ISO-certified infrastructure, and periodic vulnerability assessments, remained the foundation of our cyber resilience architecture.

# **MARKETING AND COMMUNICATION** 

FY2026 saw IndusInd Bank’s Marketing and Communications function strengthen brand visibility, customer engagement, and business growth through differentiated propositions, strategic partnerships, and digital-first initiatives. Two key highlights during the year were the ‘Sukoon Wali Banking’ campaign for Indus Care, highlighting the Bank’s specialised proposition for senior citizens, strengthening engagement with this segment, and the launch of Indus StartUp Banking, a comprehensive banking platform designed to support startups from inception to scale. Together, these initiatives reinforced the Bank’s customer-centric approach and commitment to serving evolving customer needs across segments. 

Beyond our flagship propositions, we enhanced customer engagement through strategic partnerships and expanded our payment ecosystem. The League, expanded our payments ecosystem through co-branded credit card launches, and drove retail growth through festive lending, card campaigns, and customer awareness initiatives such as ’Jaankaar Bano, Jagruk Raho’. The function also amplified IndusInd Bank’s purpose-led agenda through impactful **Beyond Banking** initiatives, including support for ‘Cricket for the Blind’, Holistic Rural Development Programme, Women Farmers Connect, and sustainability-led campaigns such as **#WalkForADrop** . Together with MSME and Wholesale Banking outreach, industry thought leadership, branch activations, and high-visibility branding initiatives, these efforts strengthened the Bank’s brand equity, stakeholder connect, and reputation as a responsible and inclusive institution. 



_Sukoon Wali Banking_ , the flagship campaign for Indus Care, showcased IndusInd Bank’s commitment to convenient, personalised banking for senior citizens. 



Through Indus StartUp Banking, the Bank aims to catalyse entrepreneurial ambition, empower innovators, and contribute meaningfully to shaping India’s next generation of high growth enterprises.

In FY2027, we will continue to advance our digital-first approach, creating seamless, contextual, intelligent, and secure experiences across the customer lifecycle. Anchored in trust and innovation, we are committed to shaping intuitive and future-ready banking experiences that evolve with the changing needs of our customers.

## **ENRICHING EMPLOYEE EXPERIENCE** 

We closed FY2026 with 46,694 permanent employees, an increase from the prior year, reflecting targeted hiring in retail banking, risk, technology, and compliance. We also completed key leadership appointments, new heads onboarded for Retail Banking, Global Markets, Risk, and Technology, reinforcing the senior layer that will drive our next phase of growth. 

Learning and development remained central to our talent agenda. Skill upgradation training reached 78.75% of employees, with female participation at a strong 91.77%. Performance and career development reviews covered 84.71% of employees, up from 78.29% in FY2025, reflecting a more consistent and structured approach to talent conversations across the organisation. 

We continued capability-building journeys for branch managers, credit officers, and risk professionals, aligning individual competencies with evolving regulatory and strategic priorities. Our Indus Evolve e-learning platform supported this through structured modules on business ethics, code of conduct, cybersecurity, governance, and ESG. Notably, 100% of Board members attended training during the year, covering IT and cybersecurity, corporate governance, risk management, and ESG. 

Our employee experience philosophy remained anchored in empathy, transparency, and enablement. Quarterly town halls and operational reviews maintained a strategic connection between leadership and the workforce. The INDY helpdesk, accessible via the PULSE intranet and Indus1 mobile app, served as the primary channel for employees to raise and resolve HR queries spanning onboarding, payroll, and lifecycle events. 

Our grievance redressal framework ensured structured, timebound resolution, with Branch Heads responsible for closing complaints within 15 days and clear escalation pathways beyond that. Reflecting this framework’s effectiveness, zero complaints related to working conditions or health and safety were filed by employees during FY2026. Recognition through service awards, peer appreciation, and performance spotlights continued to be a meaningful lever of engagement across the organisation.

# **PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT** 

We handle all reported cases in compliance with the Prevention of Sexual Harassment Act, 2013. FY2026 saw 31 complaints received under POSH, down from 53 in FY2025, of which 14 were upheld. One case remained in progress as of March 31, 2026, closing subsequently in May 2026. Employees found in violation face appropriate disciplinary action, with all cases managed in full confidence and with procedural rigour. POSH complaints as a percentage of female employees fell to 0.31% from 0.60% in FY2025. 

# **SUPPORTING WELLNESS AND PURPOSE** 

Employee wellness spends as a percentage of total revenue rose to 0.16% from 0.14% in FY2025, a measured but genuine commitment to employee health. All permanent employees are covered under health and accident insurance, and all 9,295 permanent women employees are covered under maternity benefits. 

Our Occupational Health and Safety Management System continued to embed safety practices across operations. Fire safety training and evacuation drills were conducted at 44 highrise buildings and across 100% of branches in all zones, with full participation including outsourced staff. No major safety incidents, injuries, or fatalities were reported during the year, and no Lost Time Injury events were recorded.

Our Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits discrimination, child labour, forced labour, and violations of freedom of association. # **LOOKING AHEAD** 

As we move into FY2027, our human capital agenda rests on three priorities: sustaining the leadership stability achieved this year and building depth in the layers below it; accelerating the development of a workforce equally comfortable with data and digital tools as with customer relationships; and embedding ESG commitments more deeply into how we measure, reward, and recognise performance so that sustainability becomes a lived part of our people strategy, not a separate agenda. Our people navigated a challenging year with commitment and professionalism. That is the foundation on which we will build. 

Our anti-corruption and anti-bribery framework, embedded across our Codes of Conduct for employees and senior management, recorded zero disciplinary actions for bribery or corruption during the year. Ethical conduct training reached 90% of employees through e-learning modules on Business Ethics and the Code of Conduct.

# **INTEGRATING CLIMATE RISKS INTO DECISIONMAKING** 

Climate risk has become an integral consideration in our decision-making processes, influencing client evaluation, product structuring, and operational risk management. During FY2026, we further strengthened the integration of climaterelated risks within our enterprise risk management framework. 

We enhanced our assessment of physical risks, including extreme weather events such as heatwaves, droughts, and floods, across key geographies, while continuing to monitor transition risks arising from regulatory developments, market dynamics, and evolving stakeholder expectations across our lending portfolio. Climate risk oversight is now embedded within senior management deliberations and Board-level risk governance. In parallel, we have initiated scenario analysis and climate stress testing for identified priority sectors to progressively align internal risk models with globally accepted frameworks. 

# **ENVIRONMENTAL AND SOCIAL MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (ESMS)** 

IndusInd Bank has implemented a comprehensive and integrated ESMS system that mandates the evaluation of wholesale banking loan proposals above a certain credit threshold for ESG risks. A comprehensive review of ESG risks is performed alongside credit risks before final credit approval. Credit proposals from high-risk industries undergo an in-depth ESG Risk Assessment by the sustainable banking unit and is recommended to the ESMS Committee for approval. The sustainable banking unit provides recommendations for monitoring and reporting of ESG risks associated with lending to high-risk projects/entities. 

# **OPTIMISING RESOURCES AND REDUCING ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT**

**MANAGEMENT DISCUSSION & ANALYSIS** 

# **1. MACROECONOMIC AND BANKING ENVIRONMENT** 

During the year 2025-26, the Indian economy faced external headwinds and shocks in the form of a sharp increase in tariffs amidst a shift in the US trade policies and geopolitical tensions with conflict in West Asia triggering an energy price surge. Supported by fiscal measures and monetary policy easing, the Indian economy remained resilient. While domestic drivers of private consumption and public capital spending steered growth, external sector contribution dropped. Adequate foreign exchange reserves and a flexible exchange rate helped the economy withstand the adverse external spillovers. That in turn allowed the domestic policies to focus on supporting growth. Rationalisation of the goods and services tax (GST) rate structure along with lower monetary policy rates and easy financial conditions helped drive private consumption, credit demand, and overall economic activity, especially during the second half of the year. Macro-economic and financial stability along with benign inflation also helped to underpin the domestic demand. National income estimates using the new base year 2022-23, placed real GDP growth at 7.7% in FY2026 compared to 7.1% in the year before. Global economic activity displayed resilience too, despite high import tariffs, elevated policy uncertainty, and geopolitical tensions. The final impact of the US tariff measures turned out to be less severe than initially anticipated. Fiscal support in advanced economies and technology-related investments and trade aided growth. A military conflict in the Middle East, which flared up in March, is going to test resilience of the global and the Indian economy. 

Domestic macroeconomic policies remained focused on strengthening the short-term and long-term growth impulses. On the fiscal policy front, a comprehensive review of the GST rate structure was undertaken in September, to simplify it and to further reduce internal trade frictions while providing a boost to consumption by lowering average rate. The new labour codes were implemented in November, which will help improve labour market flexibility and attract investments in labour intensive manufacturing sectors while strengthening the social security net. Benign inflation allowed the easing of the Repo rate by 100 bps over the year. Lower interest rates helped support urban consumption and investor sentiment. Trade agreements were announced with UK, EU, Oman, and 



New Zealand providing greater, and duty-free access to Indian exports while opening domestic markets to imports and investments from these regions. These wide-ranging policy measures aided in countering the adverse effects of US import tariffs on Indian exports, which were raised to 50% by August and reduced to 18% subsequently with India and US pursuing a bilateral trade agreement. Recognising India’s strong longterm growth prospects and structural improvement in public finances, rating agency S&P upgraded the country’s sovereign rating to BBB in August, marking first such upgrade in 18 years. 

Macroeconomic stability was further reinforced by the government reducing its budget deficit while maintaining focus on capital expenditure. In a major shift, the Budget for FY2027 changed the fiscal anchor to Debt-to-GDP, with a target of reaching 50+/-1% by March 2031. This moves away from targeting fiscal deficit to GDP ratio and will help strengthen the countercyclical role of the fiscal policy, by balancing the growth imperative with fiscal consolidation. Otherwise, the budget retained a capex focus with spending on capital formation kept at 3% of GDP. Along with a successful fiscal consolidation, price stability through the flexible inflation targeting framework for monetary policy is providing the necessary condition for sustaining high growth. During the year, the National Statistics Office (NSO) released a new CPI series with base year 2024, which incorporated the latest consumption pattern and made methodological and data improvements. Headline CPI inflation eased to an average of 2.1% during FY2026 from 4.6% in FY2025, helped by low food inflation and benign core inflation. With inflation easing towards the lower end of the target band, reduction in the Repo rate cut was frontloaded towards the first half of the year. 

Along with lower policy rates, the RBI also infused durable liquidity worth ₹13.80 trillion via open market bond purchases, a 100 bps CRR cut, and USD/INR swaps. That helped counter the impact of liquidity drain over the second half of the year, due to dollar sales by the RBI to support the Rupee and an increase in currency-in-circulation. Liquidity infusion helped create conditions conducive to meet the credit needs of the commercial sector. In the rates market, the sovereign bond yield curve steepened over the year, as short-end rates eased helped by lower Repo rate, while yields for medium and longer tenors rose. Large supply of government bonds, especially by the state governments, and with signals of a prolonged pause on monetary policy combined with a flare up in oil prices over the last quarter of the year, pushed long-term bond yields higher. 

In the banking sector, credit growth continued to record strong growth, enabled by strong economic activity during the second half of the year. Growth in bank credit accelerated to 16% y-o-y as on March 31, 2026, from 11% a year ago. Personal loans and the services sector continued to drive the overall credit growth during the year. Within the services sector, NBFCs remained the largest recipient of bank credit. Industrial credit growth, at 15% y-o-y remained above its long-term average, with credit to MSME segment witnessing sustained robust expansion. Credit growth in the infrastructure sector also picked up over the year. 

90 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26 

**Corporate Overview** 

On the external front, headwinds increased over the year. The current account remained in deficit on the back of rising merchandise trade deficit, while net FPI equity outflows exceeding $16 billion, pushed the overall Balance of Payments (BoP) into deficit too. The CAD as a percentage of GDP stood at 0.6% for the year, same level as the year before. While the goods trade deficit widened on higher imports growth and stagnant exports, net services trade surplus helped keep the CAD well within manageable levels. The Indian Rupee depreciated by 9.9% against the US dollar on the back of imposition of punitive tariffs by the US and the BoP deficit rising to around 0.6% of GDP. The RBI’s foreign exchange reserves increased by about $23 billion over the year, helped by valuation gains of $46 billion on its foreign assets and gold reserves. India’s overall external fundamentals remained healthy with adequate foreign exchange reserves buffer. Country’s net international investment position improved to -6.9% of GDP by end-December, from -8.7% at the end of March 2025. 

Downside risks to growth and economic activity and upside risks to inflation have intensified following a surge in oil prices driven by the West Asia conflict, and with the closure of Strait of Hormuz. 

Higher commodity and oil prices can lead to higher inflation and subdued demand, especially in commodity importing emerging economies, with currency depreciation pressures exacerbating the impact of higher energy and food prices. In response to this supply shock, the Central Government and the RBI stepped up support measures to contain the fallout on the wider economy, sectors impacted and livelihoods. Gradual normalisation of Strait of Hormuz and energy supply from the Middle East, following an MOU between US and Iran extending the ceasefire, will also help temper the headwinds. Much still depends on the duration and the intensity of the lingering energy price and supply shock. Given its domestically oriented nature along with policy support already in place and space available for more if required, the Indian economy can withstand the adverse spillovers from a short duration energy supply disruption. Still heightened uncertainty around the geopolitical and supply risk around the West Asia conflict calls for nimble policy response to ensure macroeconomic and financial stability. Measures announced by the government and the RBI in June will not only help build foreign exchange buffers and stabilise the Rupee, but will also help support the credit needs of commercial sector.

# **2.2  Business Performance Highlights** 

FY2026 was a year of stabilisation, transition, and strategic recalibration for the Bank. Against a backdrop of evolving macroeconomic conditions and internal transformation, the Bank prioritised strengthening its foundations over near-term growth. The Bank focused on balance sheet recalibration, leadership succession, asset quality improvement, and stronger governance, while laying the foundation for long-term value creation through the implementation of a refreshed strategic roadmap. 

## **Balance Sheet Recalibration with Enhanced Granularity** 

During the year, the Bank focused on optimising the balance sheet and improving its structural resilience. This included consciously moderating growth, rationalising lower risk-adjusted return businesses, and re-allocating capital towards granular and higher-quality segments. 

On the liabilities side, the Bank made steady progress in enhancing deposit granularity through a continued focus on retailisation and customer-led deposit growth. The share of retail deposits, as per Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), improved to 47.9% from 46.6% in the previous year, reflecting reduced reliance on bulk sources. 

On the asset side, the Bank adopted a selective, risk-calibrated approach, leading to moderated growth. The loan book declined by 8% y-o-y, driven by a conscious run-down in microfinance amidst an adverse asset quality cycle, alongside tightening of credit underwriting, and rationalisation of select large corporate exposures with sub-optimal risk-adjusted returns. The portfolio mix shifted towards secured retail, SME, and granular corporate segments. 

Overall, these actions resulted in a more granular and resilient balance sheet, positioning the Bank for sustainable growth. The Bank continues to maintain strong capital and liquidity buffers, with a CRAR of 17.48%, CET 1 of 16.20% and quarterly average LCR of 118%, providing ample capacity to support future growth. 

## **Leadership Transition** 

FY2026 witnessed a significant leadership transition phase, with the Bank strengthening its senior management team and organisational structure in line with its evolving strategic 

priorities. The Bank onboarded key leaders across businesses and control functions, including Retail Banking, Wholesale Banking, Risk, Technology, Finance, Internal Audit, and Human Resources. With the leadership team now largely in place, the Bank benefits from their diverse experience and strong execution focus. 

In parallel, the Bank undertook an organisation-wide structural realignment, including integration of retail distribution channels, enhancement of branch-led delivery, and strengthening of data and digital capabilities. Together, these initiatives ensure that the leadership architecture and operating model are closely aligned with the Bank’s refreshed strategic roadmap, supporting sharper execution and improved accountability. 

## **Asset Quality** 

During the year, asset quality remained stable across key portfolios, excluding micro loans. Core portfolios such as vehicle finance, SME, secured retail, and wholesale banking demonstrated resilience, with slippages remaining broadly range bound. However, the adverse microfinance cycle continued to play out in FY26 as well, resulting in elevated credit costs during the year. The Bank responded through tightened underwriting standards, strengthened collection frameworks, and prudent portfolio management. Encouragingly, the microfinance portfolio has begun to show early signs of recovery, with declining slippages, reduction in early bucket delinquencies, and improving collection efficiency. These trends indicate that the portfolio is progressing towards normalisation, providing confidence that credit costs are nearing their peak, supporting a transition towards stable and calibrated growth. 

## **Financial Outcome** 

Financial performance during FY2026 reflects the Bank’s conscious focus on strengthening the foundation before than pursuing growth. The Bank reported a consolidated pre-provision operating profit of ₹9,180 crore and a Profit After Tax of ₹889 crore for the full year. Profitability was impacted versus prior year due to loan book moderation, adverse loan mix, and elevated credit costs, primarily driven by stress in the microfinance portfolio. 

With growth gradually resuming, asset quality trends improving, and credit costs moderating, the Bank is well positioned for a meaningful improvement in profitability from FY2027 onwards.

# **Way Forward: P.A.C.E. Strategy to Drive Sustainable Growth** 

In FY2026, the Bank articulated its three-year strategic roadmap—P.A.C.E.— which provides a clear framework to drive sustainable and profitable growth: 

- h **Protect the Endowments:** Strengthen and preserve core franchises including vehicle finance, rural banking, and corporate relationships. 

- h **Accelerate Key Priorities:** Build a granular and lower-cost deposit base, scale SME and mid-market businesses, and improve efficiency. 

- h **Customer Centricity:** Deliver a unified ‘One IndusInd’ experience through digital innovation and superior service delivery. 

- h **Execution Excellence:** Drive a culture of strong execution discipline, sharper accountability, and cost efficiency. 

# **Overall** 

FY2026 represents a year of deliberate reset and transition, with the Bank taking decisive steps to recalibrate its balance sheet, strengthen governance and compliance frameworks, and align its organisation for the future. 

With a strengthened leadership team, improving asset quality trends, and a clearly defined P.A.C.E. strategy, the Bank is well-positioned to rebuild growth momentum, enhance stakeholder confidence, and deliver sustainable long-term value.

# **5. CONSUMER FINANCE DIVISION** 

The Consumer Finance Division (CFD) focuses on vehicle financing, the main domain expertise of the Bank. CFD has a healthy market share across product segments, deep customer penetration, and a well-managed business franchise. 

The CFD extends funding for a wide range of Vehicles/ Equipment, which includes Heavy, Light, and Small Commercial Vehicles used for Goods and Passenger Applications, Auto loans, Two-Wheelers, Tractors, and Construction Equipment such as Excavators, Loaders, Tippers, Cranes, etc. Finance is extended for both, new and used assets in all the above segments. Low cost / Affordable Housing Loans are being offered in CFD enabling participation in the ‘Housing for All’ project, a key focus area of the Government of India. 

CFD handled around 3 million loans with a loan outstanding of ₹1,02,715 crore in FY2026 as against ₹97,898 crore in FY2025, 5% increase over previous year. Light Commercial vehicles recorded robust growth with 12% growth over previous year with advances of ₹13,864 crore in FY2026 as against ₹12,361 crore in FY2025 followed by Small Commercial vehicles which recorded a 9% growth over the previous year at ₹4,692 crore from ₹4,311 crores. 

CFD disbursed 8.56 Lakh loans in FY2026 amounting to ₹48,127 crore as against ₹48,374 crore in the previous year. Tractor funding increased to ₹3,169 crore in FY2026 as against ₹2,682 crore in FY2025. Commercial vehicle segment encompassing Medium and Heavy Commercial Vehicles, Light Commercial Vehicles, and Small Commercial Vehicles recorded a disbursement of ₹20,650 crore in FY2026 as against ₹19,485 crore in the previous year. Auto loan disbursements were at ₹10,909 crore in FY2026 for New Vehicles and ₹3,353 crore for Used Vehicles. Construction Equipment disbursements were at ₹6,330 crore in FY2026 as against ₹6,879 crore in FY2025. Two-wheelers showed a major reduction in disbursement to ₹2,736 crore from ₹4,061 crore in FY2025 as underwriting norms were made more stringent and sourcing restricted to low delinquency branches.
